summary: A revised Telnet protocol proposal from the committee, circulated for comments. Unless comments arrived within two weeks, they would not be considered for the official Telnet document. It lists the earlier notes it builds on. It was replaced by RFC 495.

plainLanguage.summary: This proposal describes how a user at one host could interact with a remote host through Telnet. It uses a shared Network Virtual Terminal character format and defines control signals.

subtitle: A 1971 Telnet proposal built around a shared Network Virtual Terminal.

tldr.problem: Users needed a way for a terminal at one host to act like a terminal connected directly to another host, without every host knowing every terminal type.
tldr.mechanism: The proposal defines a Network Virtual Terminal using 7-bit ASCII sent in 8-bit bytes, plus control signals and implementation duties for using and serving sites.
tldr.outcome: RFC 158 was a proposal circulated for comments and was obsoleted by RFC 495.

today: RFC 158 updated RFC 139, was updated by RFC 318 and was obsoleted by RFC 495. It is a historical proposal rather than the final Telnet specification.

sections.title: Purpose of the Telnet Protocol
sections.content:
The Telnet committee circulated this document to solicit comments, evaluation and requests for modification. The committee considered the proposal adequate for initial implementation.

Telnet is described as a third-level protocol that makes a terminal or process at a using site appear logically equivalent to a terminal directly connected to a serving site. The design aims to minimize how much each host must know about other hosts.
sections.plainLanguage: The proposal lets a user at one host interact with a remote host as if a terminal were connected there. It aims to reduce host-specific knowledge.

sections.title: Protocol Levels and Sites
sections.content:
The RFC distinguishes Level 1 host-IMP protocol, Level 2 host-host protocol performed by NCPs, and Level 3 communication within a host between its NCP and processes. The Telnet process runs at Level 3 at a using site, while the Telnet server runs there at the serving site.

The protocol uses the NCP, an Initial Connection Protocol and an 8-bit byte size on the permanent connection.
sections.plainLanguage: Telnet runs above the network's host-to-host exchange. A using site runs the client process, and a serving site runs the server.

sections.title: Network Virtual Terminal and Control Signals
sections.content:
The Network Virtual Terminal uses full 7-bit ASCII transmitted in 8-bit bytes with the high-order bit set to zero. A line ends with carriage return followed by line feed. The serving site is initially assumed not to echo input to the using site.

Telnet control signals use 8-bit codes with the high-order bit set to one. The RFC assigns codes for data type, break or attention, no-op, echo behavior and hiding input.
sections.plainLanguage: The shared terminal format carries 7-bit ASCII in 8-bit bytes. Control signals use codes with the high bit set.
